title: It is I (Mark 6:45–52)
hook: walking on the lake at night: take heart, it is I, do not be afraid

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crowd like sheep without a shepherd, and five loaves in the disciples' hands. Your line was you give them something. What little did you give? Day one hundred eighty-four.

Straight after the feeding, Jesus sends the disciples off in the boat ahead of him, sends the crowd home, and climbs a hill alone to pray. Night falls. Out on the lake, the wind turns against them. They row, and row, and get nowhere. Hours of it. Arms burning, the shore not getting any closer. You know that kind of night, even if you've never held an oar: a problem you've been rowing against since sundown. And then, somewhere between three and six in the morning, someone sees a figure on the water. Walking. Today: it is I.
screen: `ALONE ON THE HILL TO PRAY.` → `ROWING AGAINST THE WIND.` → `A FIGURE ON THE WATER.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible: "he saw them toiling in rowing; for the wind was contrary unto them: and about the fourth watch of the night he cometh unto them, walking upon the sea, and would have passed by them." He saw them. From the hill, in the dark, he's been watching them struggle. The fourth watch is the last stretch of the night, before dawn. And then a strange phrase: he would have passed by them. Readers have puzzled over it. Many hear an echo of the old stories where God passes by Moses on the mountain and Elijah at the cave, showing himself as he goes. The disciples think it's a ghost, and they scream. And he speaks at once: "Be of good cheer: it is I; be not afraid." Take heart. It is I. Don't be afraid. In Greek, it is I is two words, ego eimi, which can also mean simply, I am. Many Christians hear in it the name God gives Moses at the burning bush: I am. Then he climbs into the boat, and the wind stops. You might expect joy. Mark gives us something more honest: they were utterly astonished, "For they considered not the miracle of the loaves: for their heart was hardened." They'd just seen five thousand fed, and it hadn't sunk in. Mark keeps showing us disciples who don't quite get it, which is comforting for anyone who doesn't either. And Mark's version has no Peter stepping out onto the water. That's in Matthew. Here it's just Jesus, the dark, the wind, and three phrases for frightened people: take heart, it is I, don't be afraid.
screen: `HE SAW THEM TOILING IN ROWING.` · `HE WOULD HAVE PASSED BY THEM.` · `IT IS I — EGO EIMI, I AM.` · `THEIR HEART WAS HARDENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say take heart to someone. Settle, and breathe. Picture someone rowing against the wind right now. A friend with a long night behind them and more ahead. Someone whose arms are tired. Hold them in mind. Imagine standing near them and saying, simply, take heart. You're not alone in this. If you pray, you can pray the words from the story for them: be of good cheer, be not afraid. Then choose how you'll actually say it today: a message, a call, a note. The bell holds the time.
It is I. What Jesus says to frightened men in a boat before dawn. In Greek, ego eimi, which can also mean I am.
Your line: take heart, it is I. Today, say take heart to one person who's rowing against the wind. Day one hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Many Christians turn to this story in times of fear or long struggle, and the words be of good cheer, it is I, be not afraid are often read at services for the sick and the grieving.

fork.setup: it's nearly dawn. you've rowed all night against the wind. a figure is walking toward you across the water. what do you do?
fork.reveal: they cry out, thinking it's a spirit. he answers at once: be of good cheer: it is I; be not afraid.

original.note: Greek: it is I, or simply I am. Many hear the name God gives at the burning bush.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle about walking on water.
what it means: Jesus sees his friends struggling in the dark, comes to them, and says take heart, it is I, don't be afraid.
what a scholar hears: ego eimi, I am, and he would have passed by them, both echoes of how God shows himself in Israel's scriptures.

notes: Fourth watch (Roman reckoning) about 3–6 a.m.; confirm.
'Would have passed by them' as an echo of theophany (Exodus 33, 1 Kings 19) attributed to 'many'; confirm.
ego eimi / Exodus 3:14 ('I AM') link attributed to 'many Christians'; confirm.
The index's 'take heart' renders the KJV 'be of good cheer'; both used.
